title: What is a phone tree? How It Works, Setup, and Templates
summary: Learn how a phone tree works and how to set one up for faster, more convenient customer service.
body_markdown:
You know that moment when you realize you double-booked tomorrow’s appointments and need to reschedule right away? Your panic turns to relief when you call and discover the business uses a phone tree. With just a few quick taps on the keypad, you have a new appointment time.


A phone tree is an automated call routing system that guides customers to the right department or information using voice prompts and keypad selections. It’s like having a virtual receptionist that never takes a coffee break.


If you’re wondering how to give your customers the same convenience, keep reading. In this guide, we’ll show you the benefits of having a phone tree and how to set one up to handle[high call volume](https://www.quo.com/blog/high-call-volume/) . We’ll also give you a few templates for different types of phone trees so you can choose the best option for your business.


##


**What is a phone tree?**


A phone tree, also called a phone menu, call tree, interactive voice response (IVR) menu, or[auto-attendant](https://www.quo.com/product/auto-attendant) , is an automated system that answers incoming calls and routes callers to the right person, department, or information. It plays a recorded greeting, then uses keypad presses or voice commands to move callers through a series of options. For multi-level menus, each choice opens specific sub-menu options until the caller reaches their destination.


Customers can use phone trees to:


- Check your business hours or location
- Contact customer support
- Ask your sales team for a quote


It’s like having an automated[virtual receptionist](https://www.quo.com/product/virtual-receptionist) that fields calls and handles simple inquiries. This lets your team handle a large number of calls as your business grows.


Want to learn more? See our guide:[What is a virtual receptionist](https://www.quo.com/blog/what-is-a-virtual-receptionist/) ?


### **Phone tree vs IVR vs auto-attendant vs AI receptionist**


People often use these terms interchangeably, and modern phone systems often combine them. But each still does something different.


A phone tree is the menu itself. An auto-attendant answers the call and plays the menu.[IVR](https://www.quo.com/blog/what-is-ivr/) adds voice recognition and, in advanced setups, self-service. An AI receptionist goes a step further and holds a natural conversation instead of reading a fixed list of options.


What it is What it does Best for


Phone tree The branching menu structure that callers move through Routes callers to people, departments, or information based on their choices Any business that wants callers to route themselves


IVR An auto-attendant with voice recognition Understands spoken selections and, in advanced setups, handles self-service tasks checking bank balances Businesses with high call volume or repeat self-service requests


Auto-attendant The automated system that answers calls and plays your menu Greets callers and routes them by keypad input or time of day Small teams that need simple, reliable routing


AI receptionist An AI voice agent that talks with callers in natural language Answers common questions, captures caller details, and takes messages After-hours coverage, overflow calls, or acting as a first point of contact for callers


In Quo, you can access all four capabilities. Build your phone tree with a phone menu step, let callers choose by keypad or keyword, and route calls to[Sona](https://www.quo.com/sona) when your team is busy or away from the office.


##


**How a phone tree works**


Now let’s look at how phone trees work from your customers’ perspective.


The first thing customers hear when they call is a pre-recorded greeting with menu options. Based on their response, the system automatically routes the call to the right destination. This could be another pre-recorded message with information like business hours or to a specific person, department, external line, or AI receptionist.


Unlike traditional phone systems that required receptionists to route every call manually, automated phone systems let callers reach their destination with:


- **Touch tone navigation.** Callers press keypad numbers to select options
- **Interactive voice response.** Callers say where they want to go, and the system understands their intent
- **Hybrid approach.** Combines keypad inputs and IVR for more flexibility


You control where calls go by setting up routing rules. Calls can connect to ring groups, individual extensions, voicemail, or overflow to AI-powered or live answering services.


##


**Phone tree examples**


Your phone tree can have two or more levels, depending on your business structure:


### **Basic phone tree**


A customer hears the greeting, presses or says a single option, and goes directly to that information or department. These work well for small businesses that need to route callers to sales, support, or billing. Callers can quickly reach the right representative without navigating a complex menu.


### **Multi-level phone tree**


Customers select an option that takes them to a sub-menu with additional options. For example, they may choose “Orders” from the main menu and hear sub-menu options like “Check order status,” “Track an order,” or “Questions about your order.”


These work well for businesses with multiple service offerings, departments, or locations. Callers reach the right place without feeling overwhelmed by too many choices.


Keep reading to find out how to set up single- and[multi-level phone menus](https://www.quo.com/product/auto-attendant/multi-level-auto-attendant) .


### **Conditional phone tree**


A customer calls, and your phone system uses if/then rules to route the call based on details like the time of day or who’s calling. An if/then rule, also known as a conditional statement, tells programs or systems to act in certain ways when specific conditions are met.


These rules can be simple or complex:


- **Simple.** *If* a customer calls after business hours and they aren’t a saved contact, *then* the system sends them to an AI receptionist that answers basic questions using your business’s information. If the caller is a saved contact, they’re sent down a different call routing path.
- **Complex.** *If* a customer is tagged as a VIP in your contacts, *then* the system routes the call to a dedicated account manager or, if you’re a small company, perhaps the CEO.


Either way, callers skip the phone menu and reach the right destination faster.


##


Benefits of a call tree for small businesses


**


A phone tree directs you to the information you need right away, rather than making you wait on hold or going through multiple[call transfers](https://www.quo.com/product/call-forwarding/call-transfer) .


Your customers want the same experience. According to the Salesforce Sixth Edition State of Service report,[77% of customers expect immediate interaction](https://www.salesforce.com/content/dam/web/en_au/www/documents/pdf/state-of-service-sixth-edition.pdf) when they call a company. A phone tree system meets that expectation by:


- **Reducing wait times.** Callers get the answers or support they need faster.
- **Blocking spam.** Robocallers can’t get through an IVR or press buttons, so your team isn’t wasting time on unwanted phone calls.
- **Automatically routing calls.** Menus quickly connect incoming callers to the right person, department, or information.
- **Scaling easily.** Start with your main number, then add numbers for departments like sales or tech support as your business grows.
- **Streamlining support.** Fewer transfers mean customers get help faster, improving[first call resolution](https://www.quo.com/blog/first-call-resolution/) rates.
- **Delivering important information.** Pre-recorded greetings can share updates like holiday closures or special promotions, giving customers the most up-to-date information when they call.
- **Building a professional image.** Even if you’re a two-person team, a phone menu gives the impression of a larger organization, which builds trust.


##


**How to set up a phone tree in 5 simple steps**


Ready to get started? Follow these five steps to create your first telephone tree.


### **1. Audit your call patterns**


Start by reviewing your call history to identify common customer questions, peak call times, and pain points in the current experience.


In Quo, you can[audit calls](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-audit/) with:


- **AI-powered call transcripts and summaries.** Quickly understand conversations without listening to every recording.
- [Call tags](https://www.quo.com/product/ai/call-tagging) **.** Review tags for customer sentiment, whether it’s positive, negative, or neutral.
- [Call analytics](https://www.quo.com/product/analytics) **.** Identify times with peak call volume.


These insights help you determine which issues you can resolve through self-service menu options and which require routing to a live representative.


### **2. Design your call flow**


Your[call flow](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-flow/) is a visual map of what happens when a person calls. Quo’s drag-and-drop builder makes it easy to create a custom call flow that includes a phone tree.


A basic call flow usually includes business hours and either connects customers with a rep or sends them to voicemail if no one is available. With a phone tree, customers get more detailed options to direct their calls.


Quo lets you set[ring groups](https://www.quo.com/features/ring-groups) to get customers to a rep faster:


- **Simultaneous groups** ring all team members at once.
- **Random groups** ring reps in no particular order.
- **Custom groups** send call notifications to specific reps first.


You can also set up after-hours routing rules to send customers to a different phone menu or directly to voicemail so you never miss a call.


### **3. Add a menu greeting and options**


Limit your phone menu to three to five options. If your business outgrows that, consider setting up submenus or simpler department-specific menus.


Using[IVR systems](https://www.quo.com/blog/best-ivr-system/) makes menus even more accessible by letting customers speak their selection instead of using the dial pad.


### **4. Record a greeting**


Your phone tree greeting should do two things in under 30 seconds: let callers know they’ve reached the right business and explain how to navigate the menu so they can get the help they need quickly.


Record separate greetings for during and after business hours. For example, your during-hours greeting might be: *“Thank you for calling \[business name\]. For sales, press one. For customer support, press two. For billing questions, press three. To speak with someone immediately, press zero.”*


An after-hours greeting should include your regular hours of operation, when customers can expect a response, and alternative contact options for immediate support.


If you want to give after-hours callers more than a voicemail box, add a menu option that connects them to Sona. Our AI voice agent answers common questions, captures caller details, and takes messages, so your team can follow up first thing the next business day.


### **5. Test and refine your phone tree**


Before launching your phone menu, put yourself in your customers’ shoes and go through every option. Ask yourself:


- Is the information accurate and easy to understand?
- Are the options simple to navigate?
- Does each option lead to the correct destination?
- Are all inboxes set up and working properly?
- Do any options trap customers in an endless loop with no way to speak to a rep?


Fix anything that’s confusing or broken, then test the menu again. Once you’re confident everything works smoothly, you can activate your phone tree. Remember to update your menu regularly so customers always have the most accurate and helpful experience.

##


**4 Ready-to-use phone tree templates**


Here are four[phone tree templates](https://www.quo.com/blog/phone-tree-template/) you can use to build the best call flow for your business:


### **1. Basic phone tree template**


- **Greeting.** *Thank you for calling \[company name\]. Please choose from the following options so we can connect you with the right department.*
- **Menu options.** *Press one for Sales, two for Customer Support, three for Billing, or four for General Inquiries. To repeat this menu, press five.*
- **Live help option.** *Press zero at any time to speak with a team member who can assist you.*
- **Voicemail.** *We’re currently unable to take your call. Please leave a message with your name, phone number, and reason for calling. We’ll get back to you within one business day.*


### **2. Customer support phone tree template**


- **Greeting.** *Thank you for calling \[company name\] support. Please choose from the following options so we can connect you with the right representative.*
- **Menu options.** *For technical support, press one. For customer service, press two. For order status, press three. For general questions, press four. To hear this menu again, press five.*
- **Submenus.** If needed, create sub-menus to direct customers to specific information or departments. For example, after selecting “Order Status:” *Press one to check your order status. Press two to report a problem with your order.*
- **After-hours support.** Consider using an[AI voice agent](https://www.quo.com/product/ai/voice-agent) like Quo’s Sona to handle after-hours calls. It can answer basic questions, capture contact information, and gather details for faster follow-up.
- **Customer satisfaction survey.** Offer callers the option to receive a text message with a link to a satisfaction survey after their call. Use the feedback to refine your phone tree and overall customer experience.


### **3. Sales phone tree template**


- **Greeting.** *Thank you for calling the \[company name\] sales team. Your call is important to us. Please choose from the following options to reach the right representative.*
- **Menu options.** *If you’re a new customer and would like to place an order, please press one. If you’re an existing customer and have questions about your order, please press two. For questions about your bill or to pay an existing balance, please press three. If you’d like more information about our products, please press four. For our latest promotions, please press five. To speak with a sales representative, please press six or stay on the line.*
- **Auto-text messages for missed calls.** If no representative is available, give customers the option to receive an SMS with an inquiry form so you never miss a lead.
- **After-hours voicemail or AI agent.** When you’re closed for the day, route calls to a different greeting or an AI answering service. An AI agent can prompt customers for specific details, record messages, and summarize the conversation for follow-up.


### **4. Emergency phone tree template**


- **Greeting.** *You’ve reached \[company name\]. If this is a medical emergency or a life-threatening situation, please hang up and dial 911. For urgent \[service-specific\] issues, please stay on the line and select from the following options.*
- **Menu options.** *If you’re dealing with an urgent issue that can’t wait until business hours, press one. For non-urgent inquiries or to request a follow-up, press two.*
- **Escalation path.** Route urgent calls to an emergency contact or on-call staff member. For non-urgent calls, route them to an AI agent like Sona.


### **5. Bilingual phone tree template**


- **Greeting.** *Thank you for calling \[company name\]. For English, press one. Para español, oprima el dos.*
- **Menu options.** After the caller chooses, a sub-menu can let them select specific options to route callers to a destination. For example, your English menu might say, *“For sales, press one. For customer support, press two. For billing, press three. To hear this menu again, press nine.”* Your Spanish menu might say, *“Para ventas, oprima el uno. Para soporte al cliente, oprima el dos. Para facturación, oprima el tres. Para escuchar este menú de nuevo, oprima el nueve.”*
- **Live help option.** Route each language path in that sub-menu to a ring group of teammates who speak that language and are specialized in those specific types of inquiries and let callers press zero in either sub-menu to reach a person, not an AI receptionist.
- **After-hours support.** Route calls to Sona to answer calls in English, Spanish, or French. Just know that Sona can’t switch languages mid-call. Set its language to match the menu path that leads to it.


##


**8 Common mistakes to avoid in automated phone trees**


The goal of a phone tree is to give customers the best experience every time they call. With that in mind, here are some mistakes you should avoid.


### **1. Overly complicated menu**


Keep your phone menus simple and easy to navigate. More than three to five options can overwhelm customers. This is especially true when you want to route callers to specific departments, rather than just sharing basic information like business hours, location, and seasonal announcements.


If you need more options, use submenus in a multi-level phone menu to organize them logically. This helps callers find the right department quickly and makes[transferring calls](https://www.quo.com/blog/transfer-calls/) more accurate.


### **2. No default option or way to repeat the menu**


Always include a way to repeat the entire menu in case customers miss their option the first time around.


You should also have a default option for customers who don’t make a selection, such as routing them to an operator or a specific team.


Use a simple message like: *“For all other inquiries, please stay on the line to be connected to the next available representative.* ”


### **3. No menu option to reach a live rep**


There are some questions a menu can’t answer. Make it easy for callers to reach a live person by including an option like: *“Press zero or say ‘representative’ to speak with a team membe* r.”


### **4. Not using shared numbers or fallback options**


Shared numbers let multiple reps handle incoming calls. Customers are more likely to connect with someone on the first try, which improves their experience and creates more business opportunities.


When call volume spikes, use ring groups to ring team members in batches or enable an AI agent like Sona to handle missed calls.


### **5. Not giving reps context**


Give your team the context they need to offer better support. Tools like Quo’s phone tree software show reps which option a caller selected when they come in through your phone menu.


This is especially helpful if one team handles all your calls. Knowing what kind of help a customer needs sets the stage for a better experience.


### **6. Not including voice command options**


Callers with disabilities may prefer voice commands instead of selecting menu options on the keypad. Support voice menus with options like *“To reach Sales, say ‘Sales’ or press one.”*


Busy callers who multitask also appreciate voice commands because they can navigate the menu without stopping to tap numbers.


### **7. Not including self-serve options**


According to Gartner,[73% of customers use self-service options](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-08-19-gartner-survey-finds-only-14-percent-of-customer-service-issues-are-fully-resolved-in-self-service) at some point when interacting with a company. Let your phone menu handle basic questions and tasks like:


- Checking business hours or location
- Tracking order status
- Viewing account balances


Businesses that provide self-service find that these options free reps to focus on more important calls and tasks.


### **8. No conditional call routing**


If every caller is served the same phone menu, VIP clients and after-hours callers must sort through options that don’t fit their needs, resulting in a poor customer experience. Conditional call routing will help you route calls based on who’s calling and when they call. For example, a VIP contact can be routed directly to their account manager, while after-hours callers can be routed directly to Sona.

To add a phone tree step to your default call flow:


1. Go to **Settings** and **Phone numbers** , then select the phone number you want to set up a phone tree for.
2. Scroll to the **Call flow** section, then click **Edit call flow.**

7. Once you’ve chosen how many menu options you want, you can customize the path for each option. By default, the call flow builder will add a **Ring users** step after each menu option. ##


**FAQs**


**What is the purpose of a phone tree?**


A traditional phone tree helps route calls quickly and efficiently so customers can get answers or reach the right person without long wait times.


**Do people still use phone trees?**


Yes. Businesses still use phone trees to automate phone answering, improve call routing, and enhance the customer experience. Automated systems also support scalability as your call volume increases.


**How much does a phone tree system cost?**

You also get access to other features like AI call summaries and transcripts, call transfers, ring orders, and HubSpot and Salesforce integrations.


**What’s the difference between manual and an automated phone tree?**


The term “phone tree” can mean different things.


A manual phone tree is a calling chain: one person calls a short list of contacts, and each contact calls the next few people on the list. Schools, churches, and workplaces have long used manual phone trees for crisis communication, like weather closures or safety alerts.


Today, many organizations replace manual calling chains with mass notification or emergency notification systems. These automated calling systems send pre-recorded messages or texts to large groups at once. Some businesses also use them for outbound tasks like appointment reminders.


This guide focuses on inbound phone trees, i.e., the automated phone menus that answer and route calls that come into your business.


**What are some alternatives to creating a phone tree?**


If a traditional phone tree doesn’t fit your business needs, consider these alternatives:


– Direct dial extensions for small teams
– AI receptionists or answering services that understand natural language requests
– Simple auto-attendants that route calls based on basic criteria like time of day


**How many options should each phone tree menu have?**


Keep it to three to five options per menu level. If you need to offer more categories, consider adding multiple levels rather than cramming everything into one long menu.


**How do I reduce phone tree abandonment?**


Offer the option to speak with a human immediately — (typically *“Press zero to reach a representative”* — keep menus under 30 seconds, and test your phone tree from a caller’s perspective.


**Should my phone tree be different for after-hours calls?**


Yes. Create a separate after-hours greeting that clearly states your business hours, keeps options simple, offers emergency routing if applicable and routes to an AI agent like Sona to handle common questions and take messages.
